craft_claim: Irreverent energy scales with how firmly the breached register is policed — a violation reads as daring only while the prohibition behind it is still felt as real.

supporting_evidence.location: Perspectives on Psychological Science 4(2):153-161, p. 153 and abstract
supporting_evidence.note: Taboo words are defined and sanctioned by institutions of power (religion, media) and prohibitions are reiterated in child-rearing — the charge of a breach comes from the institutionally maintained prohibition it crosses.

supporting_evidence.location: Whole-work citation (SE vol. VIII; chapter locators unverified)
supporting_evidence.note: Jokes are economical because they save the inhibitory cost of forbidden material — the forbidden register supplies the energy the joke borrows.
Humor requires an actual violation (something must be genuinely crossed) plus benignity — a breach of nothing produces no charge at all.

counterevidence.note: Taboo-word use is commonplace (a stable set of about ten words accounts for most public swearing), so for many audiences the breach is habitual rather than daring — irreverence aimed at a register the audience no longer feels as policed lands flat.
When a breach falls outside the recognized license, audiences police it as failed or offensive humor rather than counting it as daring (see clm-tone-irreverent-licensed-frame).

scope: Registers whose protection is felt by the specific audience: religious solemnity, institutional dignity, decorum around death or body, platform politeness norms.
exceptions: Sacred registers that the writer's own audience has already abandoned give no charge — breach of a dead taboo is just vocabulary.
The mechanism concerns register-prohibition, not group membership; targeting a people rather than a register is governed by clm-tone-irreverent-prejudiced-norm-backfire.
